title: God Crucified: How the Cross Reveals Who God Is

keyTerms.d: Bauckham’s phrase for what the New Testament does, repeatedly and across independent authors: it places Jesus on the Creator’s side of the line Jewish monotheism drew between God and everything else — God’s throne, God’s acts of creation, God’s eternal name, and, most tellingly, God’s worship. The framework is influential but not uncontested: James D. G. Dunn and James F. McGrath have questioned how sharply its boundary can be drawn, and Larry Hurtado preferred to frame the data as devotional practice. Nothing depends on the vocabulary as such; it depends on what the worship evidence shows.

The same two Hebrew roots, “be high” (rûm) and “be lifted up” (nāśā’), stand together of the Lord enthroned (Isaiah 6:1), of the Servant (52:13), and of “the One who is high and lifted up” (57:15). Read side by side, the God who is high and lifted up makes his dwelling with the crushed, and the crushed Servant is described in the very words of the throne-vision.

A Jewish interpretive habit later rabbis would list among their rules: reading together passages that share a distinctive word. That early Christian readers used it to join Isaiah 52:13 and 6:1 is Bauckham’s proposal — a plausible reconstruction rather than an attested report.

In the Greek Old Testament the Servant of Isaiah 52:13 will be “lifted up” and “glorified” — two verbs John uses again and again of the cross. For John the lifting up on the cross is the exaltation: the humiliation is where the glory shows.

Christ “emptied himself” by adding — taking the form of a servant and veiling his glory; the Greek names no thing he emptied himself of. Not that he set aside, lost, or diminished his deity: he remained what he was and took up what he was not.

Because the Son is one person with two natures, what belongs to either nature may truly be said of the one person. So the New Testament can say the rulers “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8) — naming the person by his divine titles and predicating of him what he underwent in his human nature. The phrase is the church’s later articulation, not a New Testament term.

Constantinople II (553): “our Lord Jesus Christ who was crucified in the flesh is true God and the Lord of Glory and one of the Holy Trinity.” It concerns the one person of the Son crucified “in the flesh,” and it is orthodox: neither the error that the Father suffered (patripassianism) nor the error that the divine nature itself suffered.

The classical teaching that the divine nature as such does not suffer. Gavrilyuk argues that for the Fathers it functioned as a qualifier marking God’s transcendence over creaturely passion, held together with a real suffering of the Son in the flesh. The question is vigorously debated: the passibilist view associated with Moltmann became common among theologians in the twentieth century, while a substantial recent literature has retrieved the classical position.

derive.q: Paul preserves an Aramaic prayer, Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!”, untranslated in his Greek-speaking churches — so the worship of Jesus is…?
derive.ans: very early — and it is the decisive marker
derive.why: That the invocation survives in Aramaic is the point. It carries us back behind Paul’s Greek to the Aramaic-speaking Judean church — to the very first community, calling on the risen Jesus as the Lord who will come, among Jewish believers who would have regarded worshiping any creature as blasphemy.

derive.q: Isaiah’s crushed Servant will be “high and lifted up” — the very words of the throne-vision — and John says Isaiah “saw his glory and spoke of him” — so the exaltation of the crucified Servant is…?
derive.ans: told in the language of YHWH’s own throne (one strong reading, not a consensus)
derive.why: John quotes Isaiah 53:1 and Isaiah 6:10 within three verses and then says Isaiah “saw his glory.” By itself the Servant’s exaltation does not make the Servant divine — Isaiah’s God exalts the humble. It is John who draws the further inference, assigning the glory of the throne-vision to Jesus. Bauckham’s specific reading is a distinctive proposal, not a consensus.

derive.q: The Philippians hymn applies Isaiah 45:23 — YHWH’s oath that to him alone every knee shall bow — to the one who descended to “death on a cross” — so the cross is…?
derive.ans: on the path to the name, not an obstacle to it
derive.why: The hymn does not say he became worthy of the divine name in spite of the cross. It places the cross on the path to the name. And the “therefore” of verse 9 rewards the self-humbling of one who was already “in the form of God”: on the orthodox reading the descent reveals the divine character rather than suspending the divine nature.

derive.q: In Revelation an angel twice refuses the worship John offers; the Lamb, “standing, as though it had been slain,” receives it without protest — so the one who shares the worship of the Creator is…?
derive.why: The new song is sung to the Lamb precisely because of his death — “Worthy are you… for you were slain.” The Lamb is not worshiped in spite of the wounds. He is identified by them; and by the book’s end the city has one throne, “the throne of God and of the Lamb.”

derive.q: If the one who hangs on the cross is personally the Son of God, his self-giving to the point of death is the act of a divine person done in his human nature — so the cross discloses…?
derive.ans: not that God is mortal, but what kind of love God is
derive.why: What the Son undergoes in the flesh — hunger, wounds, death — he undergoes in his human nature, not in the divine nature as such; but the self-giving is his own free act. And since the Son is one God with the Father and the Spirit, it tells us who God is: not a power that saves itself, but a love that gives itself.

derive.q: Grant all of it: the first Christians read the cross this way. Does that, by itself, prove the claim is true?
derive.ans: no — that turns on whether God vindicated the crucified one
derive.why: That the first Christians read the cross this way is a historical finding; whether they were right depends on whether God vindicated the crucified one, which is the question the resurrection evidence, beginning with the creed Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 15:3–7, is meant to answer.

honestState.p1: That the earliest Christians worshiped Jesus very early, within a Jewish monotheistic frame, is widely granted, though how to describe it is not: Bauckham’s “divine identity,” Hurtado’s “devotional pattern,” and James F. McGrath’s agency model are live, competing accounts of the same data. Bauckham’s specific reading of the Isaiah passages is a distinctive proposal — suggestive and well grounded in John’s own juxtapositions, but one strong reading, not a consensus. Divine impassibility is vigorously debated, and the interpretation of the cry of dereliction remains contested among New Testament scholars.
honestState.fairness: The developed creedal vocabulary came later: the New Testament hands us the data — the throne, the name, the worship, the tensions — but not the fourth-century grammar that later systematized it. The pre-Pauline dating of the Philippians hymn is itself debated (Gordon Fee argues Paul composed it), gezerâ shāvâ is a reconstruction rather than an attested report, and Moltmann’s question — whether a God who cannot suffer is a spectator — deserves respect even where the classical faith declines his answer.
honestState.verdict: What does not depend on any of these disputes is the textual pattern itself: in Philippians, in John and in Revelation, the self-humbling and death of Jesus are told in the language of God’s own glory, throne and worship, and Mark makes that death the place where Jesus is first confessed by a human being as the Son of God. So the objection that a crucified man cannot reveal God does not hold as a presumption, and, while philosophers still debate how fully the two-natures account succeeds, a formal contradiction in the claim — made of one person in two natures — has not been shown. In the self-giving of the Son, who is truly God and truly man, we see what God is like. It does not, by itself, prove that the claim is true; that is the resurrection question.

order: The earliest Christians included Jesus within the unique identity of the one God of Israel.
The Jesus they so included was the crucified one: his self-humbling and death are told in the language of God’s own exaltation, throne and worship.
Therefore — since self-giving that belongs to God’s identity is not foreign to who God is but discloses it — the earliest Christians read the cross as a revelation of who God is.

props.t: the earliest Christians included the crucified Jesus within the identity of the one God
the humiliation told in the language of God’s own throne and worship
“death on a cross” on the path to the name above every name
the slain Lamb worshiped with the one on the throne
the claim can be stated without heresy: one person in two natures
the divine nature as such suffered and died
the Trinity was torn apart at the cross
the Isaiah echo is a scholarly consensus

cards.q: State step 1 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: The earliest Christians included Jesus within the unique identity of the one God of Israel. The “divine identity” framework is influential but not uncontested; nothing depends on that vocabulary as such. It depends on what the worship evidence shows: that the first Christians gave Jesus the devotion Jewish monotheism reserved for God alone.

cards.q: State step 2 — the heart of the argument.
cards.a: The Jesus they so included was not only the exalted and pre-existent Lord but the humiliated and crucified one: the New Testament tells his self-humbling and death in the very language Israel’s Scriptures use for God’s own exaltation, throne and worship. In three places it does this; in a fourth, Mark, the death itself becomes the moment of confession.

cards.q: State step 3 — and why it needs a fence.
cards.a: If the one who belongs to God’s identity is the one who humbled himself to death on a cross, then that self-giving is not foreign to who God is; it discloses it. The step is only as safe as the Christology that governs it: the eternal Son of God, without ceasing to be God, took a complete human nature and in that nature suffered and died. The cross does not mean that the Father was crucified, that the divine nature as such bled or perished, or that the Trinity was torn apart.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the earliest Christians read the cross as a revelation of who God is. It does not, by itself, prove that the claim is true — that depends on whether God vindicated the crucified one, the resurrection question. It does not settle how the cross saves. And it is not a theodicy: it does not explain why this child suffers this way.

cards.q: Where does Isaiah’s throne meet Isaiah’s Servant — and what is the limit?
cards.a: Isaiah saw “the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (6:1); the crushed Servant too shall be “high and lifted up” (52:13); and John says Isaiah “saw his glory and spoke of him” — of Jesus (John 12:41), and uses the Servant’s two Greek verbs, “lifted up” and “glorified,” for the cross. Limit: by itself the Servant’s exaltation does not make the Servant divine — Isaiah’s God exalts the humble. It is John who draws the further inference, and the reading is one strong reading, not a consensus.

cards.q: What does the Philippians 2 hymn do with “death on a cross”?
cards.a: It places “death on a cross” on the road to the name above every name, and applies to Jesus Isaiah 45:23 — the text in which YHWH swears that to him alone every knee shall bow. It does not say he became worthy of the divine name in spite of the cross. On the orthodox reading the descent reveals the divine character rather than suspending the divine nature.

cards.q: Why does the angel who refuses worship sharpen Revelation 5?
cards.a: In the very same book an angel twice refuses the worship John offers and redirects it to God (19:10; 22:8–9); the Lamb receives it without a word of protest. And the Lamb is not worshiped in spite of the wounds. He is identified by them: the figure who shares the worship of the Creator is the slaughtered one.

cards.q: Where in Mark is Jesus first confessed by a human being as the Son of God — and what moves the confession?
cards.a: At his death, by a Roman officer: “Truly this man was the Son of God!” What moves him, on Mark’s telling, is above all the manner of a death. In the ancient world a crucified man was the opposite of divine, yet Mark chooses that moment, and no other, for the confession his whole book has been driving toward.

God the Son, crucified in the flesh: the eternal Son of God, without ceasing to be God, took a complete human nature and in that nature suffered and died. Not the Father, and not the divine nature as such. The Second Council of Constantinople required Christians to confess that the one “crucified in the flesh is true God and the Lord of Glory and one of the Holy Trinity” — neither the error of saying the Father suffered nor the error of saying the divine nature as such suffered.

cards.q: How can the New Testament say the rulers “crucified the Lord of glory” without heresy?
cards.a: Paul writes that the rulers “crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8); Peter, “you killed the Author of life” (Acts 3:15). Neither means that glory or life itself died. Both name the person by his divine titles and predicate of him what he underwent in his human nature. Later theology called this the communication of properties: because the Son is one person with two natures, what belongs to either nature may truly be said of the one person. Put in a line: God the Word suffers in the body that is his own, while the divine nature is incapable of suffering.

cards.q: Does “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” mean the Father abandoned the Son?
cards.a: No. The Son was not torn from the Father and the Trinity was not divided: the Father never ceased to love the Son, and the union of the persons was never broken. The forsakenness is real, borne in the Son’s human experience, not a severing within the one God. Jesus prays the opening line of Psalm 22, and in praying it he enters the depths of human god-forsakenness for us.

cards.q: “Isaiah 52:13 and 6:1 share a phrase, not a meaning” — what is granted, and why does the argument stand?
cards.a: Granted: nothing claims that Isaiah intended a cross; the reading-together mechanism is a reconstruction; “high and lifted up” is used of proud men. But in Isaiah 2 that human loftiness is exactly what the LORD humbles — which makes the Servant’s exaltation in the throne-vision’s words more striking, not less. And the argument does not stand on the echo: John, the Philippians hymn and Revelation 5 make the same pairing of humiliation and divine worship. The verbal echo is corroboration; the convergence of witnesses is the case.

obj.q: A crucified man died what Josephus called “the most wretched of deaths” — a slave’s death, and to a Jew a death cursed by God. A crucified Messiah is nearly a contradiction in terms; a crucified God is a scandal, not a revelation.
obj.model: Paul names that very objection — “a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles” — and his answer is not to soften the offense but to relocate wisdom: “the foolishness of God is wiser than men.” The scandal is conceded as a scandal; what is denied is that our sense of what is fitting for God is the measure of God. That is not a license to believe anything: the claim must still be coherent and vindicated. And there is a historical point, with its limits: inventors do not sabotage their own inventions, so the offensiveness of the cross explains why no one would fabricate it. It does not, by itself, show that the first Christians were right to see God revealed there; for that, a further event is needed — the vindication they claimed had occurred.

obj.q: This reads later theology back into the texts. On Bart Ehrman’s account the earliest followers held that God exalted the man Jesus, and where a pre-existent Christ appears he was at first a subordinate divine being, God’s chief angel; the co-equal God of Nicaea is the later step. And James Dunn read the Philippians hymn as Adam Christology, a contrast between two men.
obj.model: Concede what is true: the developed creedal vocabulary came later, and the communication-of-properties language is the church’s later articulation, not a New Testament term. But the disagreement is not really about dates — Ehrman himself finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul’s letters — it is about what kind of being the earliest Christians took him to be. The evidence answers with the earliest worship: the Philippians hymn, widely regarded as pre-Pauline (Gordon Fee argues Paul composed it, but the worship-of-Jesus datum stands either way), applies an exclusive-worship text of YHWH to Jesus and places “death on a cross” on the road to the name above every name. Against Dunn, Wright and Fee argue that the hymn describes one already “in the form of God” before “taking the form of a servant” — a transition Adam never made. The development is in the clarity, not in the substance.

obj.q: Either the one on the cross is impassible God, in which case he did not truly suffer, or he truly suffered, in which case he is not impassible God. “God crucified” is a square circle.
obj.model: The classical reply refuses both horns, for neither allows the distinction the creeds draw: the one divine person, God the Son, truly suffers in his human nature, while the divine nature as such does not. That is not a contradiction of the circle-and-square kind, because it does not affirm and deny the same thing of the same subject in the same respect; it is a claim about one person with two natures, and philosophers have argued at book length that the charge of formal incoherence does not go through. Whether two-natures accounts fully succeed is debated among philosophers; the point is that the charge of formal contradiction is contested, not obvious. A mystery is not a contradiction.

obj.q: Take the cry at face value: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” is the cry of a man whose hopes had collapsed. Jesus died in despair.
obj.model: Part of this should be granted. The cry is raw, and its anguish is real — on the orthodox account, the real anguish of the Son in his human experience, not a severing within the one God. But the despair reading requires setting aside the narrative Mark actually wrote, in which Jesus three times predicts his death, says he came “to give his life as a ransom for many,” and in which the cry stands within five verses of the centurion’s confession. One may judge Mark’s framing to be theology rather than history; that is a further argument, and it rests partly on wider questions, including whether the resurrection happened. Grant, as many historians do, that the cry is authentic precisely because it was awkward: the dying man still addresses God as “my God” in the opening line of Israel’s own lament, and lament prayed to God is the speech of trust under anguish, not its abandonment. Whether that trust was vindicated is the resurrection question.

unseen.q: John’s “lifted up” is just a double meaning — raised on a pole. The glory comes afterwards, at the resurrection. The cross is the humiliation Jesus passes through on the way to glory, not the place where God’s glory is shown.
unseen.model: The double meaning is real, and John spells it out: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself,” which he glosses, “He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.” But John does not let the two senses come apart. In the Greek Old Testament the Servant of Isaiah 52:13 will be “lifted up” and “glorified” — two verbs John uses again and again of the cross — and as the cross approaches he writes, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified”; “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him.” For John the lifting up on the cross is the exaltation. He does not tell a story of humiliation followed by glory; he tells a story in which the humiliation is where the glory shows. And he sets Isaiah 53 and Isaiah 6 side by side and says that Isaiah “saw his glory and spoke of him.” So the objection does not hold as a reading of John: on his own terms, the cross is where the glory is seen.
